title: Euclid XI.Def.15-28: A cube is a solid figure contained by six equal squares.
summary: Euclid XI.Def.15-28: A cube is a solid figure contained by six equal squares.
body: Euclid, Book XI, XI.Def.15-28, as worded on this page: "A cube is a solid figure contained by six equal squares. An octahedron is a solid figure contained by eight equal and equilateral triangles. An icosahedron is a solid figure contained by twenty equal and equilateral triangles. A dodecahedron is a solid figure contained by twelve equal, equilateral and equiangular pentagons." The argument printed under that statement begins: "Definition 25 Definition 26 Definition 27 Definition 28 These are four of the five regular solids. The tetrahedron is not mentioned here since it is a certain triangular pyramid. It’s called simply the “pyramid” in Book XIII. The regular tetrahedron is constructed in proposition XIII.13 , the cube in XIII.15 , the octahedron in XIII.14 , the icosahedron in XIII.16 , and the dodecahedron in XIII.17 . These five are shown to be the only regular solids in proposition XIII.18 ." The page is David E. Joyce's text of the Elements. He describes that text as similar to Heath's translation of Heiberg, and slightly less literal.
said_by: Euclid, in David E. Joyce's text of the Elements at Clark University
